dedupe_keys.name: england extreme heat and cause specific risk of hospital admission 2008 to 2019

description: This case study measures how summer heat raises the risk of unplanned hospital admission for adults in England across a broad set of conditions. The authors, from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and Imperial College London, published it as an open-access journal article. They used records of over 4 million NHS in-patient admissions in the summers of 2008 to 2019 to build daily time series for 32,837 census areas and paired them with high-resolution temperature data in a case time series design with distributed lag non-linear models, comparing the 99th with the 50th temperature percentile. Coverage is the adult population of England. The article is free under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Caveats: admissions data are confidential and not released with the article, only summer months were studied, and heat effects vary locally. The conditions studied contributed more than 3.7 million admissions, 42 percent among people aged 75 and over, and extreme heat raised risks for many causes, including acute renal failure (relative risk 1.37) and metabolic disorders (1.28). Simulation uses: estimating heat-driven surges in hospital demand for capacity planning and climate adaptation of health services. Related records: the Portugal heatwave admissions study (case_study-portugal-heatwaves-hospital-admissions) and the Swiss heat admission cost study (case_study-switzerland-heat-hospital-admission-costs) cover other countries.
